questions.question: A key is one or more attributes that ______ other attributes.
questions.explanation: Keys determine other attributes. That single word is what connects keys to normalization.

questions.question: What two jobs do keys do?
options: Speed up sorting, and compress storage
Ensure each row is uniquely identifiable, and establish relationships among tables
Encrypt sensitive columns, and audit access
Replace the need for a data dictionary
questions.explanation: Unique identification plus relationships between tables (and therefore data integrity).

questions.question: Match each type of key to its definition.

pairs.right: The attribute or combination that uniquely identifies a row
A key composed of more than one attribute
Any key that can uniquely identify a row
A minimal superkey — nothing can be removed from it
The primary key of one table placed in another to create a common attribute
A key used strictly for data retrieval purposes

questions.explanation: Note the relationship: every candidate key is a superkey, but a superkey is only a candidate key if it's minimal.

questions.question: A candidate key is a ______ superkey — one from which no attribute can be removed and still identify a row.
questions.explanation: Minimal. Add an extra column to a candidate key and you still have a superkey, but no longer a candidate key.

questions.question: A SHIFT_LOG table has columns (badge_no, shift_date, start_time, end_time, post_name). A worker can appear only once per date. Which is a superkey but NOT a candidate key?
options: (badge_no, shift_date)
(badge_no, shift_date, post_name)
(badge_no)
(shift_date)
questions.explanation: (badge_no, shift_date) already identifies a row, so adding post_name still identifies it — a superkey — but it is no longer minimal, so it is not a candidate key.

questions.question: An attribute that is part of a key is called a ______ attribute.
questions.explanation: A key attribute. Attributes that are not part of any candidate key are called nonprime (or non-key) attributes.

questions.question: Match each kind of primary key to its description.

pairs.right: A real-world identifier already familiar to end users
A made-up, artificial value such as an auto-number
A primary key built from more than one attribute

questions.explanation: A natural key is part of the day-to-day business vocabulary; a surrogate key exists only to be a key.

questions.question: Which is NOT a reason to use a surrogate primary key?
options: There is no natural key suitable as a primary key
The natural primary key would be a composite key with multiple data types
The natural primary key is too long to be usable
The table has fewer than one thousand rows
questions.explanation: Table size isn't a reason. The three listed reasons are: no suitable natural key, an awkward multi-type composite, or a key that's simply too long.

questions.question: A tool library identifies each borrower by an auto-numbered patron_id rather than by their email address. patron_id is a:
options: Natural key
Surrogate key
Secondary key
Foreign key
questions.explanation: It's made up by the system rather than drawn from the real world, so it's a surrogate key.

questions.question: Every table row must have a primary key.
questions.explanation: Each table row must have a primary key. That is entity integrity.

questions.question: The condition in which each row in a table has its own unique identity is called ______ integrity.
questions.explanation: Entity integrity: all primary key values are unique, and no part of a primary key may be null.

questions.question: Match each integrity rule to its requirement.

pairs.right: All primary key entries are unique, and no part of a primary key may be null
A foreign key is either null, or matches a primary key value in the related table

questions.explanation: Entity integrity governs the primary key of a row; referential integrity governs the foreign key pointing at another row.

questions.question: Under referential integrity, a foreign key column may:
options: Contain any value at all, checked only by the application
Contain either a null, or a value that matches a primary key in the related table
Never contain a null under any circumstances
Contain only values that do not appear in the related table
questions.explanation: Null is allowed (the relationship may simply be optional); an invalid, non-matching value is not.

questions.question: A standard example of referential integrity: a customer might not yet have an assigned sales representative — but it is impossible to have an INVALID one. What does the null represent there?
options: A data-entry error that must be corrected
An optional relationship that has not been filled in yet
A violation of entity integrity
A duplicate primary key
questions.explanation: The null marks an optional participation — no representative assigned yet. Referential integrity blocks invalid values, not missing ones.

questions.question: Enforcing referential integrity makes it impossible to delete a row whose primary key has mandatory matching foreign key values in another table.
questions.explanation: Exactly — that's why you delete children before parents. The practice database in the SQL playground will refuse such a delete if you try it.

questions.question: Which of these violates ENTITY integrity rather than referential integrity?
options: A loan row points at a patron_id that does not exist
Two rows in the patron table share patron_id 14
A branch row has a null locality_id where the relationship is optional
A foreign key column is indexed
questions.explanation: Duplicate primary key values break entity integrity. A dangling foreign key breaks referential integrity.

questions.question: The absence of any data value in a column is called a ______.
questions.explanation: A null. It can mean an unknown value, a known but missing value, or an inapplicable condition.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three things a null can mean?
options: An unknown attribute value
A known but missing attribute value
An inapplicable condition
A value of zero
questions.explanation: Zero is a real value. Null is the absence of a value — which is why it needs IS NULL rather than = 0.

questions.question: Match each catalogue-style term to what it actually describes.

pairs.right: A description of all tables in the database, created by the user and designer
A system data dictionary describing all objects in the database
The complete logical view — the full description of the database
The description of one individual table

questions.explanation: Note the distinction: the database schema covers everything; a relational schema is per-table.

questions.question: Which relationship type is the norm for relational databases?
options: One-to-one (1:1)
One-to-many (1:M)
Many-to-many (M:N)
Many-to-one only
questions.explanation: 1:M is the most common type in relational databases.

questions.question: How is a many-to-many relationship implemented in a relational database?
options: By putting a foreign key in whichever table is larger
By creating a new connecting entity in 1:M relationships with both original entities
By merging the two tables into one
By storing a comma-separated list of key values in one column
questions.explanation: A new connecting entity — a bridge/composite/associative entity — sits between them in two 1:M relationships.

questions.question: The bridge table in an M:N relationship goes by several names. Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The connecting table created to resolve an M:N relationship
Another name for that same connecting table
A third name for it, emphasising that it records an association

questions.explanation: Composite, bridge and associative all name the same thing. It includes the primary keys of the tables being linked, as foreign keys.

questions.question: What does a composite (bridge) entity contain?
options: Only its own surrogate key
The primary keys of the tables being linked, held as foreign keys
Copies of every attribute from both linked tables
Nothing — it is a view, not a table
questions.explanation: It includes the primary keys of the tables to be linked, as foreign keys — and together those usually form its composite primary key.

questions.question:
A firm needs to record which EMPLOYEEs work on which PROJECTs. An employee may be assigned many projects, and a project may have many employees.

Someone tries to do it with only the two main tables, each carrying a foreign key to the other:

• EMPLOYEE (emp_id, proj_id) — employee 1 works on projects 1, 2 and 3, so their proj_id has to read "1,2,3"
• PROJECT (proj_id, emp_id) — project 2 has employees 1, 2 and 3, so its emp_id has to read "1,2,3"

Why does this design not work?
options: Because foreign keys are not allowed in more than one table
Because a single foreign key field would have to hold several key values at once, violating the atomic attribute rule
Because the two tables would then have the same primary key
Because a table may not have more than two foreign keys
questions.explanation: One column holds one value. Writing "1,2,3" into proj_id breaks atomicity, and the same problem appears from the other direction in PROJECT — which is why an M:N needs a third table instead.

questions.question:
The M:N between EMPLOYEE and PROJECT is resolved with a bridge table, ASSIGNMENT, holding one row per pairing — (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (3,3) and so on.

In ASSIGNMENT, the columns emp_id and proj_id are:
options: Two independent primary keys
Foreign keys that together form a composite primary key
Secondary keys used only for retrieval
Surrogate keys generated by the DBMS
questions.explanation: Each is a foreign key on its own; together they form the composite primary key of the bridge table.

questions.question: In a 1:M relationship, where does the foreign key go?
options: In the table on the "one" side
In the table on the "many" side
In both tables
In a separate bridge table
questions.explanation: The foreign key always goes on the many side, referencing the primary key on the one side.

questions.question: One DIVISION operates many DEPARTMENTs; each DEPARTMENT is operated by one DIVISION. The foreign key belongs:
options: division_id in DEPARTMENT
department_id in DIVISION
In both tables, to keep them in sync
In neither — the join works without one
questions.explanation: Many departments per division means the many side is DEPARTMENT, so division_id goes there. Putting department_id in DIVISION would only allow one department per division.

questions.question: Although relational tables are independent of one another, they can be linked through common attributes — that is, foreign keys.
questions.explanation: Independent tables, linked by common attributes — that is the whole idea of the relational model.

questions.question: What is the basic building block of a relational database?
options: The index
The table
The query
The view
questions.explanation: Tables are the basic building blocks, and keys are central to using them.

questions.question: A key that is used strictly for data retrieval purposes — not to enforce uniqueness or relationships — is called a ______ key.
questions.explanation: A secondary key exists to make retrieval convenient, e.g. looking customers up by surname.

questions.question: A SEAT_BOOKING table has (performance_id, seat_code, patron_id, price_paid), where performance_id + seat_code together identify a booking. What kind of key is (performance_id, seat_code)?
options: A composite primary key
A surrogate key
A secondary key
Two separate primary keys
questions.explanation: One key made of more than one attribute is a composite key; here it's the primary key, so a composite primary key.

questions.question:
A SEAT_BOOKING table has (performance_id, seat_code, patron_id, price_paid), where performance_id + seat_code together identify a booking.

patron_id refers to the primary key of a PATRON table. patron_id is therefore:
options: Part of the composite primary key
A foreign key
A superkey
A null-only column
questions.explanation: The primary key of one table placed in another is a foreign key — the common attribute that links them.

questions.question: A foreign key and the primary key it references must have the same column name.
questions.explanation: They usually do — which is what makes NATURAL JOIN and JOIN USING convenient — but it isn't required. When the names differ, join with JOIN ... ON.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of duplicate column names across two joined tables?
options: Poor naming by the designer
The existence of a foreign key
The use of surrogate keys
Case-insensitive collation
questions.explanation: The foreign key deliberately repeats the parent's primary key name, so joining the two tables produces two columns with that name.

questions.question: In entity relationship modeling, an M:N relationship is valid at the conceptual level.
questions.explanation: Valid conceptually — but for the logical model and the actual ERD you need a bridge table.

questions.question: "In ERM, an M:N relationship is valid at the conceptual level." What must happen before it becomes a logical/physical design?
options: Nothing — it can be implemented directly
It must be resolved into a bridge table, giving two 1:M relationships
One of the two entities must be deleted
It must be converted into a 1:1 relationship
questions.explanation: Conceptually M:N is fine; logically you need the bridge table.

questions.question: ______ describes the relationship classification — 1:1, 1:M or M:N — on an ERD.
questions.explanation: Connectivity and cardinality are used together for this: connectivity labels the type, cardinality expresses the numbers.

questions.question: Database designers, however effective, are often forced to make design compromises.
questions.explanation: The clean textbook answer and the practical answer sometimes differ; real designs involve trade-offs.

questions.question: A tool library wants to record that each UNIT (a physical copy) belongs to exactly one BRANCH, while a BRANCH holds many UNITs. Which design is correct?
options: unit_id in BRANCH
branch_id in UNIT
A bridge table between UNIT and BRANCH
Merge UNIT into BRANCH
questions.explanation: 1:M with UNIT on the many side, so the foreign key branch_id lives in UNIT. No bridge table is needed unless a unit could belong to several branches at once.

questions.question: A catalogue GADGET can belong to several GROUPs (Plumbing, Measuring…), and each GROUP contains many GADGETs. What does the design need?
options: group_id in GADGET
gadget_id in GROUP
A bridge entity holding gadget_id and group_id as foreign keys
Nothing — store the group names in a text column
questions.explanation: That's M:N, so it needs a bridge entity. This is exactly the gadget_group_map table in the practice database.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the difference between entity integrity and referential integrity, and give one example of a violation of each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Entity integrity concerns the primary key of a row: every primary key value must be unique and no part of it may be null, so each row has its own identity. A violation would be two rows in PATRON sharing patron_id 14, or a row with a null patron_id.

Referential integrity concerns a foreign key: it must either be null or match an existing primary key value in the related table. A violation would be a CHECKOUT row whose patron_id is 9999 when no such patron exists.
rubric: Said entity integrity is about the primary key being unique and not null
Said referential integrity is about a foreign key matching an existing primary key (or being null)
Gave a concrete violation of entity integrity (duplicate or null PK)
Gave a concrete violation of referential integrity (a foreign key pointing at a row that doesn't exist)
questions.explanation: The short version: entity integrity looks inward at the row's own identity; referential integrity looks outward at the row it points to.

questions.question: A club tracks MEMBERs and the EVENTs they attend. A member may attend many events, and an event may be attended by many members. Describe the tables you would create, and name the key in each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Three tables.

MEMBER — primary key member_id, plus member attributes (name, contact details).
EVENT — primary key event_id, plus event attributes (title, date, venue).
ATTENDANCE (the bridge/composite entity) — member_id and event_id, each a foreign key to its parent table, and together the composite primary key. Any attribute that describes the pairing rather than the member or the event alone — for example checked_in_at — also belongs here.

The M:N is now two 1:M relationships: one MEMBER has many ATTENDANCE rows, and one EVENT has many ATTENDANCE rows.
rubric: Named a bridge/composite/associative table between MEMBER and EVENT
Said the bridge holds both member_id and event_id as foreign keys
Said those two together form the composite primary key of the bridge
questions.explanation: Recognising "many ... many" in a business rule and reaching straight for a third table is the single most reliable ERD reflex to build.
